COMMENTS: A large excavation around 30 m2 has been organised and produced many stone artefacts, small rests of forest fauna (deer, wild boar, monkey) and shells. Dates obtained from level 2 and 3 are between 9270 B.P. and 6590 B.P. These levels display a unique archaeological deposit, comprising some lithic artefacts so far unknown in South Sumatra. We identified diverse monofacial pebble tools (in chert and limestone) which were similar to the classic Hoabinhian tool-kit, called Sumatralith in the scientific litterature. These monofacial tools/Sumatraliths were produced through a shaping method and were associated with a production of flakes retouched in scrapers, notches or denticulated. The raw material was brought back from the river and was various: chert, andesit, fossilised wood, jasper, sandstone, etc.

COMMENTS: The carvings on this rock cliff are engraved on one side of a large stone wall. The monolith is oriented north-south, while the rock art itself faces west. The paintings on the rock wall are divided into six parallel rows (six walls). The carvings on these walls depict human heads, decorated with human faces and necks, with slight variations. Below these six walls is another wall with carvings depicting a masked human face without a neck. Not all of the masked images are clearly visible, as the carvings on the third and fifth walls are somewhat worn. However, the lines of the carvings still reveal the masked decorations, except on the sixth wall, which is so worn that it is difficult to recognize the shape of the painting. What is interesting about this rock art is the carving in the shape of a five-petaled flower between the first and third frames (Purwanti, 2003).

The book described the discovery of a dolmen in Muara Payang Village. Long after that publication, only in 1999 to 2002, the Palembang Archaeological Center led by Kristantina Indriastuti conducted a survey and test pit at the jar burial location. The research succeeded in finding a megalithic building complex, a jar burial complex, and an earthen fort. The megalithic remains at the Muara Payang site are tetralith arrangements, dolmen, stone seats and monolith stones.

COMMENTS: Description: Following Dubois' efforts, there appears to have been a hiatus in archaeological field research on Sumatra until 1908, when the geologist Tobler, while working for the Dienst van het Mijnwezen in southern Sumatra, identified and excavated Ulu Tjangko Cave in Jambi. He collected material including obsidian shards, bone fragments of vertebrates and human skeletal parts, including upper arm bone, femur, skull fragments, lower jaw with chin and a few loose molars (Zwierzycki 1926:63). Tobler also collected surface finds from Kikim River in Palembang Province. All Tobler's material was subsequently described by Sarasin (1914).

COMMENTS: Description: The Gunung Megang site is a cultural site of ancestral worship, consisting of stone chamber tombs, menhirs, dakon stones, stone mortars, dolmens, stone mortars, and statues. The site is a valley surrounded by hills, the area used by the local community for rice fields and plantations, and in some areas, it is still covered in scrub. Gunung Megang is composed of andesite stones in the form of blocks with a southwest-facing facade and a square plan measuring 2 x 1.9 x 1.4 m. The roof of this building consists of three stones arranged parallel by lying down at the level of the surrounding ground surface. The largest stone is placed at the front, then in the middle there are smaller boulders, while the rear is of medium size. To support the roof structure, this building has walls consisting of four sides and on one side, namely on the northwest wall, there is a painting. The northwest wall consists of two rectangular monolithic blocks, standing side by side, of relatively equal size. The painting is visible on the left-hand side of the wall, near the entrance. During heavy rainfall, water pools up to the area directly beneath the painting.
